name: Titanoboa
length_note: Estimate from vertebra size: about 12.8 m, give or take 2.2 m (Head et al. 2009). Estimated weight about 1,135 kg.
discovered: 2009, Jason Head and colleagues (fossils from the Cerrejón coal mine)
fact: Titanoboa was the biggest snake ever found - longer than a school bus - and lived in a hot rainforest about 8 million years after the big dinosaurs died out.

name: Vasuki
length_note: Estimate from 27 vertebrae: about 10.9 to 15.2 m (Datta & Bajpai 2024); the authors say the estimate is uncertain.
discovered: 2024, Debajit Datta and Sunil Bajpai (Panandhro lignite mine, Kutch, Gujarat)
fact: Vasuki is named after the serpent king that coils around the god Shiva's neck, and it may have been nearly as long as Titanoboa.

name: Gigantophis
length_note: Disputed estimate: older figures were about 9.3-10.7 m, but a 2017 study (Rio & Mannion) estimated 6.9 m, give or take 0.3 m.
discovered: 1901, Charles William Andrews (Fayum, Egypt)
fact: For over 100 years Gigantophis was thought to be the longest snake that ever lived, until Titanoboa was found in 2009.
dispute: Length estimates differ a lot between studies.

name: Madtsoia bai
length_note: Estimate: about 9-10 m. Age given here is approximate (the 'Notostylops beds' of Patagonia, Eocene).
discovered: 1933, George Gaylord Simpson (Patagonia, Argentina)
fact: Madtsoia bai was a giant constricting snake from Patagonia, and the whole Madtsoiidae family is named after its genus.

name: Madtsoia madagascariensis
length_note: Estimate: 'almost 8 m' (LaDuke et al. 2010).
discovered: 1961, Robert Hoffstetter (Maevarano Formation, Madagascar)
fact: This heavy, nearly 8-metre snake was an ambush hunter on Madagascar at the same time as dinosaurs like Majungasaurus.

name: Madtsoia pisdurensis
length_note: Estimate from vertebrae: about 5 m (Mohabey, Head & Wilson 2011).
discovered: 2011, Dhananjay Mohabey, Jason Head and Jeffrey Wilson (Pisdura, central India)
fact: Its vertebrae were found at Pisdura in India, a place famous for dinosaur fossils, and it was a close cousin of the later giant Vasuki.

name: Madtsoia camposi
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1998, Jean-Claude Rage (São José de Itaboraí, Brazil)
fact: Madtsoia camposi was found in an old limestone quarry near Rio de Janeiro that holds some of South America's oldest snake fossils.
dispute: Rage noted that putting it in the genus Madtsoia might be provisional.

name: Wonambi naracoortensis
length_note: Estimate: about 4-6 m. It survived until roughly 50,000-40,000 years ago.
discovered: 1976, Meredith Smith (Naracoorte Caves, South Australia)
fact: Wonambi was still alive when the first people reached Australia, and it is named after a giant rainbow serpent from Aboriginal stories.

name: Wonambi barriei
length_note: Estimate: under 3 m. Known from early Miocene (possibly late Oligocene) deposits at Riversleigh; the age here is approximate.
discovered: 2000, John Scanlon and Michael Lee (Riversleigh, Queensland)
fact: Wonambi barriei was a smaller, older cousin of Wonambi naracoortensis that lived in the ancient rainforests of Riversleigh in Queensland.

name: Yurlunggur
length_note: Estimate: typically about 4.5-6 m; one vertebra may come from a 7-8 m individual (speculative).
discovered: 1992, John Scanlon (Camfield Beds, Northern Territory)
fact: Yurlunggur was a big Australian constrictor named after a great serpent in Aboriginal stories of Arnhem Land.

name: Nanowana godthelpi
length_note: Small (the name means 'dwarf serpent'); no published length found.
discovered: 1997, John Scanlon (Riversleigh, Queensland)
fact: Its name starts with 'nano', Greek for dwarf, because it was a small member of a family full of giant snakes.

name: Nanowana schrenki
length_note: Small; no published length found.
discovered: 1997, John Scanlon (Riversleigh, Queensland)
fact: Nanowana schrenki shared the Riversleigh rainforests of ancient Queensland with its cousin Nanowana godthelpi.

name: Sanajeh
length_note: About 3.5 m, from a partial skeleton (Wilson et al. 2010).
discovered: 2010, Jeffrey Wilson, Dhananjay Mohabey, Shanan Peters and Jason Head (Dholi Dungri, Gujarat)
fact: Sanajeh was found fossilised coiled around a dinosaur egg next to a baby sauropod - it probably raided dinosaur nests for hatchlings.

name: Menarana nosymena
length_note: Estimate from secondary sources: about 2.4 m.
discovered: 2010, Thomas LaDuke, David Krause, John Scanlon and Nathan Kley (Maevarano Formation, Madagascar)
fact: Menarana may have dug through soil head-first, hunting small animals while dinosaurs walked above it on ancient Madagascar.

name: Menarana laurasiae
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1996, Jean-Claude Rage (as Madtsoia laurasiae, Laño, Spain); moved to Menarana in 2010
fact: This snake from Spain was first put in Madtsoia, then moved to Menarana after its cousin was found in Madagascar.

name: Herensugea caristiorum
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1996, Jean-Claude Rage (Laño, Basque Country, Spain)
fact: Herensugea is named after a dragon-serpent from Basque legends, fitting for a snake that lived alongside dinosaurs in Spain.

name: Nidophis insularis
length_note: Small; one secondary source suggests about 1 m (unconfirmed).
discovered: 2013, Ştefan Vasile and colleagues (Haţeg Basin, Romania)
fact: Nidophis means 'nest snake' - it was found right next to a nest of dinosaur eggs on an ancient island in Romania.

name: Alamitophis argentinus
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1986, Adriana Albino (Los Alamitos, Patagonia, Argentina)
fact: Alamitophis was one of several kinds of snakes slithering around Patagonia near the very end of the age of dinosaurs.

name: Kelyophis hechti
length_note: Less than 1 m - the smallest snake of its fossil site (LaDuke et al. 2010).
discovered: 2010, Thomas LaDuke, David Krause, John Scanlon and Nathan Kley (Maevarano Formation, Madagascar)
fact: Its name means 'small serpent', mixing a Malagasy word for small with the Greek word for snake.

name: Najash
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 2006, Sebastián Apesteguía and Hussam Zaher (Candeleros Formation, Río Negro, Argentina)
fact: Najash had two small back legs with a real hip, and is named after the snake in the Bible's Garden of Eden story that had legs.
dispute: An early snake not placed in any family; where it sits in the snake family tree is still debated.

name: Dinilysia
length_note: Estimate from secondary sources: about 1.8-2 m (some say up to 3 m).
discovered: 1901, Arthur Smith Woodward (Neuquén, Patagonia, Argentina)
fact: Dinilysia is one of the few dinosaur-age snakes known from whole skulls, so scientists use it to study how snake heads evolved.

name: Pachyrhachis
length_note: No published length confirmed.
discovered: 1979, Georg Haas (Ein Yabrud quarries, north of Jerusalem, West Bank)
fact: Pachyrhachis was a sea snake with tiny back legs that still had hip, knee and ankle joints - at first it was even mistaken for a lizard.
dispute: Family placement and its exact spot among snakes are debated.

name: Haasiophis
length_note: A little over 1 m (single fossil).
discovered: 2000, Eitan Tchernov and colleagues (Ein Yabrud, West Bank)
fact: Haasiophis had back legs only about 2 cm long, but they still had all their bones right down to the toes.
dispute: Some scientists have suggested it could be a young Pachyrhachis, but its skull and teeth are quite different.

name: Eupodophis
length_note: The fossil is about 50 cm long.
discovered: 2000, Jean-Claude Rage and François Escuillié (Lebanon)
fact: In 2011 scientists used super-powerful X-rays to find a second tiny leg hidden inside the rock of this 95-million-year-old snake.

name: Simoliophis rochebrunei
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1880, Henri-Émile Sauvage (Charentes, France)
fact: Simoliophis was a slow-swimming sea snake from the same family as the legged snakes Pachyrhachis and Eupodophis, living in shallow seas over what is now France.

name: Lapparentophis defrennei
length_note: Known only from three vertebrae; no length.
discovered: 1959, Robert Hoffstetter (In Akhamil, Algeria)
fact: Known from just three small backbones found in the Sahara, Lapparentophis was once thought to be the oldest snake in the world.
dispute: Later studies place it in Ophidia (the wider snake group) rather than among true snakes.

name: Seismophis septentrionalis
length_note: Known from one vertebra; no length.
discovered: 2014, Annie Hsiou, Adriana Albino, Manuel Medeiros and Raquel Santos (Cajual Island, Maranhão, Brazil)
fact: Seismophis is one of the oldest snakes known from Brazil, found on an island off the coast of Maranhão.

name: Xiaophis
length_note: The only fossil is a baby about 4.75 cm long (missing its head); adult size unknown.
discovered: 2018, Lida Xing, Michael Caldwell and colleagues (amber from Myanmar)
fact: Xiaophis is a baby snake trapped in tree resin 99 million years ago - the first baby snake ever found preserved in amber.

name: Coniophis precedens
length_note: Small; sources disagree on the length.
discovered: 1892, Othniel Charles Marsh (Lance Formation, Wyoming); redescribed 2012 by Nicholas Longrich and colleagues
fact: Coniophis had a snake's body but a lizard-like head, and probably burrowed in the soil of floodplains alongside T. rex.
dispute: A very early snake not placed in any living family.

name: Portugalophis
length_note: Estimate: about 1 m.
discovered: 2015, Michael Caldwell, Randall Nydam, Alessandro Palci and Sebastián Apesteguía (Guimarota coal mine, near Leiria, Portugal)
fact: Portugalophis was found in an old coal mine in Portugal and lived about 155 million years ago, when Portugal was a swampy coast full of dinosaurs.
dispute: Named as one of the oldest snakes in 2015, but a 2025 study argues the parviraptorids were snake-like lizard relatives, not true snakes. Still debated.

name: Diablophis gilmorei
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 2015, Michael Caldwell and colleagues (Morrison Formation, Colorado)
fact: Diablophis, the 'devil snake', lived in Colorado at the same time as Stegosaurus and Allosaurus.
dispute: A 2025 study argues it was a snake-like lizard relative, not a true snake. Still debated.

name: Parviraptor estesi
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1994, Susan Evans (Purbeck Limestone, Dorset, England)
fact: Parviraptor means 'little robber' and was found in rocks on the south coast of England.
dispute: Called a stem snake in 2015, but its describer and a 2025 study think it was a snake-like lizard relative instead.

name: Eophis underwoodi
length_note: Known only from tiny jaw pieces; no reliable length.
discovered: 2015, Michael Caldwell and colleagues (Kirtlington, Oxfordshire, England)
fact: When it was named in 2015 Eophis, the 'dawn snake', was called the oldest snake in the world at about 167 million years old.
dispute: A 2025 study treats the name as doubtful and the group as snake-like lizard relatives, not true snakes. Still debated.

name: Palaeophis colossaeus
length_note: Estimate: suggested to exceed 9 m (Rage 1983); the 2018 study by McCartney and colleagues re-estimated its size from vertebrae.
discovered: 1983, Jean-Claude Rage (Tamaguélelt, Mali)
fact: Palaeophis colossaeus was the biggest sea snake ever, swimming in a shallow sea that once flooded what is now the Sahara Desert.

name: Palaeophis maghrebianus
length_note: Large vertebrae suggest it may have been longer than any living snake (estimate, Houssaye et al. 2013).
discovered: 1952, Camille Arambourg (Ouled Abdoun phosphates, Morocco)
fact: This giant sea snake's bones show it grew fast, and its fossil vertebrae are still dug up in Moroccan phosphate mines.

name: Pterosphenus schucherti
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1898/1899 (sources differ), Frederic Augustus Lucas (Cocoa, Alabama)
fact: Pterosphenus had a flat, tall body like a ribbon to help it swim, and its bones were found next to those of early whales in Alabama.

name: Archaeophis
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 1859, Abramo Massalongo (Monte Bolca, Italy)
fact: Archaeophis may have had more backbones than any other snake known - about 565 of them (an older count says 507).
dispute: The vertebra count differs between sources.

name: Eoconstrictor fischeri
length_note: Medium to large; no single published length.
discovered: 2004, Stephan Schaal (as Palaeopython fischeri, Messel Pit); moved to Eoconstrictor in 2020 by Agustín Scanferla and Krister Smith
fact: This boa from the Messel Pit in Germany had heat-sensing pits on its lips - the oldest sign of a snake that could 'see' warmth.
dispute: The heat-sensing interpretation is the authors' reading of the fossil.

name: Boavus idelmani
length_note: Estimate for the genus: 1-2 m.
discovered: 1938, Charles Gilmore (Green River Formation, Wyoming)
fact: Boavus idelmani was found in the rocks of an ancient lake in Wyoming that also preserved fish, birds and bats in amazing detail.

name: Eoanilius europae
length_note: Small; no published length found.
discovered: 1974, Jean-Claude Rage (Phosphorites du Quercy, France)
fact: Eoanilius was a small burrowing snake from France, a distant cousin of the red pipe snake that still lives in South America.
dispute: Exact age is uncertain because many Quercy fossil sites are poorly dated.

name: Python europaeus
length_note: No published length found.
discovered: 2003, Zbigniew Szyndlar and Jean-Claude Rage (Vieux Collonges, France)
fact: Pythons once lived in Europe - Python europaeus slithered around France about 15 million years ago when it was much warmer.
dispute: Putting it in the genus Python rests mainly on one skull bone.

name: Boa blanchardensis
length_note: Estimate: 73-139 cm, a dwarf island boa.
discovered: 2018, Corentin Bochaton and Salvador Bailon (Blanchard Cave, Marie-Galante, Guadeloupe)
fact: This small boa lived in caves on the Caribbean island of Marie-Galante and disappeared around the end of the last Ice Age.
dispute: Probably extinct at the end of the Pleistocene; it may possibly have survived a little into the Holocene.
